title: Recall Score
subtitle: Topic: Recall Score · Subject: AI Evaluation and Benchmarking. Three beginner, two medium and two advanced questions, seven unique SVG teaching diagrams, balanced alternatives and a tested scikit-learn snippet.
hero:
RECALL SCORE · VISUAL STUDY

How many of the real positives did the model detect?

Recall measures coverage of actual positive examples. It emphasizes false negatives, not false positives. Explore the confusion matrix, thresholds, averaging, ranking Recall@k, and robust benchmark reporting.

questions.tag: Beginner · Recall formula and missed positives
questions.stem: What does Recall Score measure in binary classification, and how is it computed from true positives and false negatives when some real positive cases are missed?
options: Recall measures the fraction of predicted positive alerts that are correct, dividing true positives by true positives plus false positives. Its main purpose is measuring false-alarm reliability rather than missed positive cases.

Recall measures the proportion of all predictions that are correct, adding true positives and true negatives before dividing by the number of examples. Missed positives matter only through overall accuracy.
Recall measures the share of actual positives found by the classifier, using TP/(TP+FN). If 21 of 30 truly positive cases are detected and nine are missed, recall is 70%.
Recall measures how consistently a model rejects actual negatives, using TN/(TN+FP). A low score therefore indicates many false alarms even if every truly positive case was successfully detected.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Recall asks how many actual positive examples the classifier successfully detected. Its denominator counts all truly positive cases: those correctly found (TP) and those wrongly predicted negative (FN). The formula is TP/(TP+FN). If an equipment-fault detector finds 21 of 30 genuine faults, recall is 21/30=70%, with nine missed faults. Correct predictions on negative examples are not part of this calculation. High recall matters when missed events are costly, but the model may still create many false alarms.

questions.tag: Beginner · Recall versus specificity and precision
questions.stem: How does positive-class Recall Score differ from specificity and precision, and what values follow from TP=18, FN=6, TN=60 and FP=12?
options: Recall is TP/(TP+FN)=75%, specificity is TN/(TN+FP)=83.3%, and precision is TP/(TP+FP)=60%. These metrics use different denominators and describe detection, negative rejection and alert reliability.
Recall is TP/(TP+FP)=60%, specificity is TP/(TP+FN)=75%, and precision is TN/(TN+FP)=83.3%. These labels describe the same outcomes but simply use different names for the calculations.
Recall, specificity and precision all equal the fraction of correct predictions, so each is (18+60)/96=81.25%. Their apparent differences disappear when the total number of examples is known.

Recall measures only false positives, specificity measures only false negatives, and precision measures both through the total sample count. Therefore all three should increase automatically whenever classification accuracy improves.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Positive recall measures detected positives out of actual positives: 18/(18+6)=75%. Specificity, or true-negative rate, measures correctly rejected negatives: 60/(60+12)=83.3%. Precision measures correct positive predictions out of all positive predictions: 18/(18+12)=60%. Each metric answers a different operational question. In airport security screening, recall concerns prohibited items that are missed, specificity concerns innocent bags correctly cleared, and precision concerns how many inspection alerts are justified. Balanced accuracy averages recall and specificity.

With 18 true positives, 6 false negatives, 60 true negatives and 12 false positives, recall is 75%, specificity 83.3% and precision 60%.

questions.stem: How do different score thresholds influence Recall Score and precision, and why can raising a threshold make a high-precision classifier overlook important positive cases?
options: Raising a threshold always increases recall because positive predictions become more trustworthy. Precision decreases at the same time, since the classifier begins labeling more negative cases as positive.

A threshold changes the actual ground-truth labels rather than the predicted labels, so recall can rise without any new true positives. Comparing thresholds requires retraining on the final test data.

Changing a threshold alters only probability calibration, never the number of predicted positives. True positives and false negatives stay constant, so recall is unaffected even when precision changes.
Raising the threshold predicts fewer positives and can increase missed cases. In the tested example recall falls from 84.6% to 38.5% as thresholds rise, while precision increases in that sample.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A decision threshold turns classifier scores into positive or negative labels. Raising the threshold makes positive predictions more selective, potentially reducing false alarms but also missing real positives. In the tested holdout with 13 actual positives, recall is 84.6% at threshold 0.25, 69.2% at 0.50 and 38.5% at 0.75. Precision increases in this particular experiment, but it need not increase at every threshold on every dataset. A medical alert system needs a threshold informed by the costs of misses and false alarms.

questions.tag: Medium · Multiclass macro, weighted and micro recall
questions.stem: How are macro, support-weighted and micro Recall Scores computed for multiclass classification, and why can some averages conceal a class that the model never detects?
options: Macro recall weights each class according to how frequently it is predicted, while weighted recall averages classes equally. Micro recall uses only the rarest class, so it cannot hide any class-specific failures.

Macro recall pools all class confusion counts into one ratio, while micro recall averages each class separately. Weighted recall gives every label equal importance, so the scores necessarily match on imbalanced tasks.
Macro recall averages per-class detection rates equally; weighted recall weights them by true support; micro recall pools all TP and FN counts. In the example they are 54.1%, 80% and 80%.

All recall averages equal the smallest class recall because recall always emphasizes false negatives. A model failing one rare class therefore must have zero macro, micro and weighted recall regardless of its other predictions.
questions.explanation: Explanation: For a multiclass problem, treat each label as positive in turn and calculate its recall. The example yields 27/30=90% for class A, 13/18≈72.2% for class B, and 0/2=0% for class C. Macro recall averages these equally, about 54.1%. Support-weighted recall accounts for actual class counts, producing 80%. Micro recall pools detections across all classes and also gives 80% here. In single-label multiclass classification, both micro and weighted recall equal accuracy. Per-class results expose missed minority groups.

questions.stem: How can Recall Score be calculated using scikit-learn on unseen examples at several decision thresholds, while preventing preprocessing leakage and reporting false negatives correctly?
options: Standardize the complete dataset first, then split into training and testing, and tune the threshold using repeated test recall checks. This guarantees leakage-free results because the classifier itself fits only training rows.

Split labeled examples first and fit StandardScaler plus LogisticRegression inside a training pipeline. On held-out probabilities, calculate thresholded labels, confusion-matrix counts, recall_score and precision_score without refitting preprocessing.

Calculate recall by thresholding the original feature columns rather than model scores, then count all predicted negatives as false negatives. A separate training pipeline is unnecessary because recall uses only positive examples.

Retrain the entire classifier on held-out test labels for each threshold and report whichever threshold gives the highest recall. Since recall ignores false positives, these repeated test evaluations remain unbiased.
questions.explanation: Explanation: First divide the labeled examples into training and holdout sets. A scikit-learn Pipeline fits scaling and logistic regression using only the training rows. The model then produces positive-class probabilities for 65 unseen examples. The 15-line code thresholds those scores at 0.25, 0.50 and 0.75 and uses confusion_matrix, recall_score and precision_score to report the outcomes. Actual-positive support is 13, so false negatives rise as recall falls. For deployment, select the threshold on validation data rather than optimizing it on the final test set.
questions.figure:
QUESTION 05 · RECALL SCORE
scikit-learn · Three threshold evaluation 15 lines
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, recall_score, precision_score
X,y=make_classification(n_samples=260,n_features=6,n_informative=4,
    n_redundant=0,weights=[.80,.20],flip_y=.025,class_sep=1.1,random_state=37)
Xtr,Xte,ytr,yte=train_test_split(X,y,test_size=.25,stratify=y,random_state=13)
model=make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),LogisticRegression(max_iter=500)).fit(Xtr,ytr)
scores=model.predict_proba(Xte)[:,1]
for threshold in (.25,.50,.75):
    pred=(scores>=threshold).astype(int)
    tn,fp,fn,tp=confusion_matrix(yte,pred).ravel()
    print(threshold,(tp,fn,fp,tn),round(recall_score(yte,pred),3),round(precision_score(yte,pred,zero_division=0),3))

The 15-line script fits a train-only scaling and logistic-regression pipeline. It evaluates 65 test cases and reports TP, FN, FP, TN, recall and precision.

questions.tag: Advanced · Recall at k for ranked retrieval
questions.stem: What does Recall@k measure in information retrieval or RAG evaluation, and how does its denominator differ from Precision@k when examining a ranked list of results?
options: Recall@k divides relevant results in the first k positions by k, while Precision@k divides them by all relevant items in the collection. Their values therefore reverse the definitions used by binary classifiers.

Recall@k measures how many retrieved results have high model confidence, independent of whether they are relevant. Precision@k instead measures how many relevant items exist overall before any retrieval happens.
Recall@k and Precision@k are identical whenever the ranking includes at least one relevant document, because both divide by the number of retrieved results and disregard relevant items not retrieved.
Recall@k is the fraction of all relevant items recovered in the first k results. If eight items are relevant and the top five contain three, Recall@5=3/8=37.5%, while Precision@5=3/5=60%.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Recall@k asks how many relevant items a retrieval system managed to include among its first k results, relative to all relevant items in the evaluation collection. Precision@k instead divides by k. If there are eight truly relevant documents and the top five contain three, Recall@5 is 3/8=37.5%, while Precision@5 is 3/5=60%. In a RAG system, high retrieval recall may help provide enough supporting evidence to the generator. Reliable evaluation also requires sufficiently complete relevance judgments, which can be hard to collect.

questions.tag: Advanced · Undefined recall and evaluation integrity
questions.stem: When is Recall Score mathematically undefined, and how should AI benchmarks report zero-detection cases while guarding against unreliable labels and evaluation leakage?
options: Recall is undefined when TP+FN=0 because no actual positive examples exist; a zero-division reporting convention should be explicit. If positives exist but none is detected, recall is defined as zero.

Recall is undefined whenever the classifier predicts no positives, even if the evaluation set contains many actual positives. In that situation benchmarks should report perfect recall because there are no incorrect positive alerts.

Recall is undefined when false positives exceed true positives, because its denominator includes both error types. Choosing a lower threshold always fixes the numerical problem without affecting the reliability of test estimates.

Recall is always a defined number because classification libraries silently replace every zero denominator with one. Benchmark authors need not document missing classes, zero-division settings or the count of actual positives.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Recall divides TP by TP+FN, which counts actual positives. If the evaluation set has no positive examples, both counts are zero and recall is mathematically undefined. A library may report zero under an explicitly selected zero_division convention. If five actual positives exist but the model finds none, recall is exactly 0/5=0%, not undefined. Benchmarks should report class support, TP and FN, and verify label quality and split integrity. Evaluate thresholds on validation data and monitor whether class prevalence changes after deployment.
